anchor: If you don’t have them in you yet, borrow them from someone steady, as long as they won’t take advantage of that to try to run your trip for you.
text: If you go manic, psychotic (by which I mean losing your sense of reality to the point of posing a risk to yourself or others), get super paranoid, or end up worse afterward than before, those are signs to reconsider trying the same thing again, and try to figure out why that happened. Don’t try again until you understand what would make it safe.
from_source: If you go manic, psychotic (by which I mean losing your sense of reality to the point of posing a risk to yourself or others), get super paranoid, or end up worse afterward than before, those are signs to reconsider trying the same thing again, and try to figure out why that happened. Don’t try again until you understand what would make it safe.
source_section: S102 If a past trip went badly
paragraph_after:
I’m not saying you should use substances, but many people have used them when they first did self-hypnosis, contacted their inner child, or talked to their Higher Self. I’d learn the inner child work sober first, with enough Nurturer and Protector in the room before you go deep (see the inner child reparenting section). If you don’t have them in you yet, borrow them from someone steady, as long as they won’t take advantage of that to try to run your trip for you.

If you go manic, psychotic (by which I mean losing your sense of reality to the point of posing a risk to yourself or others), get super paranoid, or end up worse afterward than before, those are signs to reconsider trying the same thing again, and try to figure out why that happened. Don’t try again until you understand what would make it safe.
why: A reader who mixes substances with this work learns the signs that mean don't repeat the same trip until they know what would make it safe.
doubt: The guide's own safety sections, which the comparison wasn't given (S073, S084, S143, S144), already name mania, psychosis and paranoia as reasons to stop going deeper and get help. So the part that is new here is 'Don’t try again until you understand what would make it safe.' 'If you go manic' and 'the same thing' lean on the paragraph before for what was taken. The source goes on to say what to look at (the drug, the dosage, mindset and setting) and links his bad-trips guide, which this guide doesn't link; I left both out to keep it to two sentences. The comparison suggested a link to the inner child guide's 'Losing Touch With Reality' sections; whether to link is his call.

anchor: If you feel resistance, just meet it with love.
text: If you feel resistance, listen to it and be patient.
from_source: They might go numb, or call BS on that. If so, they might just need to see if you’re actually humble enough, and grateful enough for them, to listen to their rejection, be patient, and be open to the possibility that your Higher View is missing the trees for the forest.
source_section: S059 Invite Your Little One In
changed_from_source: Kept the guide's own opening ('If you feel resistance') and put the source's 'listen to their rejection, be patient' where 'just meet it with love' was, with 'it' for 'their rejection' because this sentence speaks of resistance. Left out 'call BS' and 'humble enough, and grateful enough', which the guide already has word for word in S080, and 'your Higher View is missing the trees for the forest', because this guide has no 'Higher View'.
paragraph_after: Gently breathe in lots of love and begin to send that love from your heart down to your inner child as you breathe out, noticing what comes up for you. If some comes back up, let it, and send it on down again, so it goes around like a loop. That part's a gift from them, and they don't owe it to you, so if nothing comes back, just keep sending yours. If you feel resistance, listen to it and be patient. If you feel or see something, just meet that with love as well. If you can't find any warmth today, just leave your hands where they are and notice what's there. Don't pretend to feel something you don't. Let it go back and forth between your heart and your inner child, like a real conversation.
why: A reader whose inner child refuses the love stops sending more at them and listens.
doubt: S080 (You get stuck in spiritual bypass), which the comparison wasn't given, already carries the source sentence nearly whole, so the caution is in the guide; this change stops S024 from telling the reader the opposite. The next sentence ('If you feel or see something, just meet that with love as well.') stays; its 'as well' used to point back to this sentence and now points back to the sending of love, so it could lose 'as well'. The source's third point, that the view from above may be missing something, isn't in this guide anywhere, and I didn't bring it in here.

anchor: And I don’t think the Higher Self has any specific wisdom.
text: And I don’t think the Higher Self has any specific wisdom that can be followed mechanically.
from_source: But where I part ways with IFS is I don’t think the Higher Self has any specific wisdom that can be followed mechanically.
changed_from_source: Kept the guide's 'And' where the source has 'But where I part ways with IFS is', since this passage isn't about IFS (Internal Family Systems). The rest is word for word.
paragraph_after: Once you have the ability to notice, and to differentiate, you don’t need to keep rehearsing it. Just work on whatever it is you need to work on (often being warm to yourself, protecting yourself and knowing what to do etc). So even though it can be useful to talk about your Higher Self, it doesn’t mean you already have all the good inner parenting functions etc that you need. And I don’t think the Higher Self has any specific wisdom that can be followed mechanically. It’s a vantage point, where more wisdom and compassion can come up, but problems can also look like they were never problems at all from up there, and that can ironically lead instead to more foolish indifference.
why: The sentence no longer reads as 'the Higher Self has no wisdom', two paragraphs after a script that asks it for help.
doubt: No doubt about the change. I left out the source's next point, that leaving all decisions to the Higher Self is spiritual bypassing: S027 already names overruling your inner child in the name of something higher as spiritual bypassing, and S132 says an inner answer isn't an order.

anchor: So when you begin talking to your inner child in a new, loving way, that dusty old script may huff and puff that what you’re doing is “fake”.
text: Keep in mind that while a critical voice might be that inherited parent script, or any outside influence with no concern for your welfare, it could also be trying to protect you from rejection or failure. It may be pointing to a real problem, but in a cruel way. Stay curious about the critical voice’s motivations, and open to any kernels of truth it points out, without accepting its insults and cruelty.
from_source: Keep in mind that while a critical voice might be that inherited parent script, or any outside influence with no concern for your welfare, it could also be trying to protect you from rejection or failure. It may be pointing to a real problem, but in a cruel way.
We want to use the Mr. Rogers reframing trick to stay curious about the critical voice’s motivations, and open to any kernels of truth it points out, without accepting its insults and cruelty.
source_section: S027 The Parent You Inherited (the first two sentences); S028 Reframe the Critic (the third)
changed_from_source: The first two sentences are word for word. The third drops 'We want to use the Mr. Rogers reframing trick to', because this guide doesn't tell the Mr. Rogers story, and starts at 'Stay curious'.
paragraph_after:
One important thing to become aware of when approaching your inner child is your inherited parent script. This is the set of rules and ways of treating yourself that you internalized as a child, mostly based on how your parent(s) treated you, and it doesn’t always sound like a voice. This is not the same as your inner adult (Nurturer, Protector, Guide) that you build up on purpose. Often this script acts as a critic or warden, telling your inner child not to cry or complain. You might be hearing, "Don't be needy! Don't embarrass us! And don't be independent." So when you begin talking to your inner child in a new, loving way, that dusty old script may huff and puff that what you’re doing is “fake”.

Keep in mind that while a critical voice might be that inherited parent script, or any outside influence with no concern for your welfare, it could also be trying to protect you from rejection or failure. It may be pointing to a real problem, but in a cruel way. Stay curious about the critical voice’s motivations, and open to any kernels of truth it points out, without accepting its insults and cruelty.
why: The reader stops treating every critical voice as the old script to answer back, and listens for what's true in it without taking the cruelty.
doubt: The guide says something close about other parts (S021: there will likely be something true in the child's complaints; S070: 'there could be something to it'; S121 on the anxious guard: 'It can be right!'), but not about the critic. The third sentence can go if he wants only the caution. I left S070's parent-script paragraph, which the comparison also named, as it is.

anchor: Still, notice it, and then look at what might be going on.
text: Let a stray thought go as just thinking. A worry that just keeps asking to be reassured can go the same way, unless it’s your inner child asking.
from_source: Let a stray thought go as just thinking, and come back to the room you’re in. A worry that just keeps asking to be reassured can go the same way, unless it’s your little one asking.
source_section: S070 Which thoughts to talk to
changed_from_source: Dropped 'and come back to the room you’re in': in this guide coming back to the room is the return from hypnosis (the script in S053 says 'coming back to the room I am in now'), so here it could be read as ending the session. 'your little one' became 'your inner child', the name S028 uses.
paragraph_after: Use parts language here too, if it helps. Often, we see a sensation or a distraction or an objection as something that needs to be explored, when in fact it might just be hunger, or reasonable skepticism about something, or a sentence that doesn’t fit. Still, notice it, and then look at what might be going on. Let a stray thought go as just thinking. A worry that just keeps asking to be reassured can go the same way, unless it’s your inner child asking.
why: The reader doesn't look into every passing thought, or keep feeding a worry that only wants to be reassured.
doubt: S081 (You get stuck in endless processing), which the comparison wasn't given, already says to let a checking thought be there without engaging with it and get on with what you chose to do, so the reassurance half is partly in the guide. The addition follows 'look at what might be going on' and narrows it; if the two read as pulling against each other, that sentence would have to change too, and I left it.

anchor: G. Stop and rest before the caring turns into another performance, and reconnect with them later to see what was helpful.
text: If these exercises start feeling like a ritual you have to complete before you’re allowed to live, stop there.
from_source: If these exercises start feeling like a ritual you have to complete before you’re allowed to live, stop there.
source_section: S089 Is It Helping? (its last sentence; the comparison's quote is from S088 Healing or Checking?)
paragraph_after: G. Stop and rest before the caring turns into another performance, and reconnect with them later to see what was helpful. If these exercises start feeling like a ritual you have to complete before you’re allowed to live, stop there.
why: The steps end on a plain rule for when to stop: when the practice has turned into something to get through before living.
doubt: I didn't carry the comparison's own quote (going back to the same wound over and over can become a search for certainty): S081 (You get stuck in endless processing), which the comparison wasn't given, already says it, with a question to ask yourself and what to do. The stop rule is the part the guide lacks, and the comparison named it too. 'These exercises' is his wording; S032 gives steps A to G no name, so here it reads as the guide's practices in general, which is what the source means.

anchor: A. Prepare yourself to tend to them with some privacy, but still able to access support if needed.
text: If being alone was a big part of what hurt during your childhood, I’d call somebody now, mess and all, since reaching toward people is part of taking care of your little one too. Even if you don’t have someone you know who wants to listen, there are warmlines for this (not hotlines unless it’s an emergency).
from_source: If being alone was a big part of what hurt during your childhood, I’d call somebody now, mess and all, since reaching toward people is part of taking care of your little one too. Even if you don’t have someone you know who wants to listen, there are warmlines for this (not hotlines unless it’s an emergency).
source_section: S007 Dip Your Toes In First
paragraph_after: A. Prepare yourself to tend to them with some privacy, but still able to access support if needed. If being alone was a big part of what hurt during your childhood, I’d call somebody now, mess and all, since reaching toward people is part of taking care of your little one too. Even if you don’t have someone you know who wants to listen, there are warmlines for this (not hotlines unless it’s an emergency). Check how much grown-up you is really in the room first. Can you take a moment before you react? When you decide something, do you follow through? If you answered "No," because right now you’re mostly still stuck identifying as the frightened little boo, hold off on the deeper conversation. Do what makes you feel adult before you try to talk to little you.
why: A reader who was hurt by being left alone is told to reach for a person before doing this in private.
doubt: 'Warmlines' is explained only by the contrast with hotlines; the source says no more about them, so I added nothing, and he may want to say what one is. The two sentences sit between the privacy sentence and the grown-up check, which makes step A long. Nothing else in the guide says this.

anchor: You can say to the guard “You don’t have to let me in, just tell me what I need to do to make it safe”.
text: If you don’t hear a little kid talking in your head, don’t invent one.
from_source: If you don’t hear a little kid talking in your head, don’t invent one.
paragraph_after: If you can tell there is a guard in the way, talk to it. You can say to the guard “You don’t have to let me in, just tell me what I need to do to make it safe”. If you don’t hear a little kid talking in your head, don’t invent one. Even if there isn’t a child part that you can talk to, you can work with whatever you are aware of. You can work on your preferences or something that you’re curious about or something that you’re willing to try as a beginner etc. and see how it goes. Work on developing a sense of who you are and reparent yourself as best you can.
why: A reader who hears no inner voice is told not to make one up, right before being told to work with whatever they are aware of.
doubt: The rest of the source passage (that 'ask' can sound like waiting for a second voice to answer) is already in the guide, in sections the comparison wasn't given or didn't connect: S005 says 'ask' and 'listen' don't mean full sentences will come, and S028 says there's no need to answer for a part. So I carried only this one sentence, and S028 comes close to it.

anchor: Some examples of answers might be “I need to know you will set boundaries,” “I need to know you will do what you said you will do,” “I need to know you won’t keep leaving,” or “I need to know you won’t think that knowing something means that you don’t need to do anything about it.”
text: If an answer tells you to act, I’d only do it if it’s loving and leaves you free. It should make sense, too. Even then, anything big or hard to undo can wait until you’re calm and you’ve checked it against what you actually know.
from_source: If it tells you to act
I’d only do it if it’s loving and leaves you free. It should make sense, too. Even then, anything big or hard to undo can wait until you’re calm and you’ve checked it against what you actually know.
source_section: S073 If it tells you to act
changed_from_source: Put the source's heading in front, as 'If an answer tells you to act,', so that 'it' has something to point to. The rest is word for word.
paragraph_after:
There may not be an answer. There may not be an answer that will help you. You may need to try asking a different question or you may just need to rest or finish your inner work for the day. If trust is actually a concern, you can try asking your subconscious “What would you need to know in order to trust me?” Some examples of answers might be “I need to know you will set boundaries,” “I need to know you will do what you said you will do,” “I need to know you won’t keep leaving,” or “I need to know you won’t think that knowing something means that you don’t need to do anything about it.”

If an answer tells you to act, I’d only do it if it’s loving and leaves you free. It should make sense, too. Even then, anything big or hard to undo can wait until you’re calm and you’ve checked it against what you actually know.
why: A reader whose subconscious does answer, and with an instruction, has a test to put it to before acting.
doubt: skip: the guide already says this, almost word for word, in S092 (Core prompts): 'If it tells you to do something, I'd only do it if it's loving and leaves you free. It would have to make sense too. And even with all that, I wouldn't do anything big or hard to undo until I'm calm and I've checked it against what I actually know.' S132 (When the subconscious speaks like an oracle) says it again: an answer isn't an order, and a big thing or one that can't be easily undone slows down and goes to the council. The comparison wasn't given either section.

anchor: If there is no child there, just work with a guard or whatever you find.
text: Old memories might come up too. They can feel totally real, but that alone doesn’t prove they happened.
from_source: Old memories might come up too. They can feel totally real, but that alone doesn’t prove they happened.
source_section: S096 Altered Can Make It Real
paragraph_after: I see a lot of connection between reparenting therapy and self hypnosis. I’d learn to do inner-child therapy sober first, in your ordinary mindstate, since that’s the one you’ll be living in, and get enough Nurturer and Protector in the room before you go deep. When you go into hypnosis, your inner child might come to you. It might show up in any form. It can be an image, a posture, a voice, a memory, an emotion, etc. It can be any age. It can be any vulnerable part of you. If there is no child there, just work with a guard or whatever you find. Old memories might come up too. They can feel totally real, but that alone doesn’t prove they happened.
why: A reader told the inner child may show up as a memory is also told that feeling real isn't proof it happened.
doubt: skip: the guide already says this in several sections the comparison wasn't given: S062 ('it isn’t a record of what actually happened'), S067 ('not everything in hypnotic imagery is literal, especially if it relates to trauma and memory'), S083 (don't use trance to prove something happened to you), S084 (reassess if you're getting more certain about unconfirmable memories), S013 and the sources note S164. One more repeat in S031 adds nothing.

anchor: Seeking counsel can slide into abdicating to an authority figure without you noticing.
text: They can know things you don’t and still be wrong for you to follow too much. The test is whether the relationship makes you more grounded, truthful, and free.
from_source: But they can know things you don’t and still be wrong for you to follow too much. The test is whether the relationship makes you more grounded, truthful, and free.
changed_from_source: Dropped the opening 'But'. The rest is word for word.
paragraph_after: On the other hand, it is possible to give your power away. Seeking counsel can slide into abdicating to an authority figure without you noticing. They can know things you don’t and still be wrong for you to follow too much. The test is whether the relationship makes you more grounded, truthful, and free.
why: The warning about handing your power to an authority comes with a way to tell when it is happening.
doubt: The guide does give ways to notice, in sections the comparison wasn't given: S009 ('it can take a no and wait') and the questions in S038 ('If I say no, what will the consequences be?', 'do I come away from them more present and grown up, or less?'). So this repeats, in other words, a test the guide has; a pointer from S133 to S038 would do the same job. For that reason I left out the source's follow-up questions (do they respect a no) and its manipulation signs. I left the 'safe adult' sentence in S019, which the comparison also named, as it is.

anchor: It has to come from a place of understanding, otherwise it can be bypassing.
text: And we don’t have to forgive first to get safe, set boundaries, hold someone accountable, get justice or get better.
from_source: And you don’t have to forgive first to get safe, set boundaries, hold someone accountable, get justice or get better.
changed_from_source: 'you' became 'we', because this paragraph is written in 'we'.
paragraph_after: We cannot force forgiveness on ourselves. It has to come from a place of understanding, otherwise it can be bypassing. And we don’t have to forgive first to get safe, set boundaries, hold someone accountable, get justice or get better. However, if we remain in the anger forever, we are allowing the injury to dictate how we live our lives in the present. So how do we hold all of this? We just remember that it can all be true at once. They really did hurt us and they still have to answer for it. Our boundary with them is crucial to maintain, especially after forgiveness which can tend to weaken it. One day we may find that we have forgiven them for not knowing better, just like Jesus did on the Cross.
why: The reader can't take the passage to mean that getting safe or getting better has to wait for forgiving.
doubt: The paragraph already says the boundary stays and that they still have to answer for it; what it lacks is that none of this waits on forgiving, which this sentence says. No other doubt.

anchor: So you might start by tracking, by discovering where the activation is, where a neutral place is, and then whether you can move your attention from one to the other, very slowly, like a snail.
text: SE’s founder, Peter Levine, uses the concepts of titration (going from the shallow end of the pool slowly deeper), pendulation (going in and out of the deep end to learn safety there), and orientation (coming out of the pool, drying off, noticing you’re safe).
from_source: He uses the concepts of titration (going from the shallow end of the pool slowly deeper), pendulation (going in and out of the deep end to learn safety there), and orientation (coming out of the pool, drying off, noticing you’re safe).
changed_from_source: 'He' became 'SE’s founder, Peter Levine,' because S124 hasn't named him; the name is from 'it’s founder, Peter Levine,' earlier in the same source section, without its apostrophe slip. The rest is word for word.
paragraph_after: If you would like more information about somatic experiencing, or even a free intro session, please see my somatic guide . In somatic experiencing (SE), you are not digging into the trauma. You learn to track. So you might start by tracking, by discovering where the activation is, where a neutral place is, and then whether you can move your attention from one to the other, very slowly, like a snail. SE’s founder, Peter Levine, uses the concepts of titration (going from the shallow end of the pool slowly deeper), pendulation (going in and out of the deep end to learn safety there), and orientation (coming out of the pool, drying off, noticing you’re safe).
why: The reader learns there is a third step after moving between the two places: coming out and noticing you're safe.
doubt: His sentence names the closing step but doesn't tell the reader to do it, and I didn't write an instruction the source doesn't have. The comparison asked for one sentence on orientation alone; his sentence brings titration and pendulation with it, and the pool arrives with no lead-in (as it does in the source). The guide does have ways to finish, in sections the comparison wasn't given: S053 (Come all the way back) is its return, and S030 and S044 say to orient yourself by looking around. S161 already credits Levine for titration and pendulation.

anchor: Also stop if the massage makes the anxiety symptoms worse, or makes you feel bad in any way, such as painful, dizzy, tingly, etc.)
text: Some massage therapies are super aggressive, like Rolfing, some are fairly aggressive still like Deep Tissue, some are medium-aggressive, like Thai massage, and some, like Swedish Massage, are quite gentle. Choose the level that feels right for you.
from_source: Some massage therapies are super aggressive in that domain, like Rolfing , some are fairly aggressive still like Deep Tissue, some are medium-aggressive, like Thai massage, and some, like Swedish Massage, are quite gentle. Choose the level that feels right for you.
changed_from_source: Dropped 'in that domain', which in the source points back to a sentence about unravelling stored tension that isn't in this guide. The space before the comma after 'Rolfing' in the source is where his link sits; the link would need carrying over with the word.
paragraph_after: Sometimes the mind is too activated for meditation to help, so you may need to work directly with the body to calm it down. Maybe get a massage, or massage a foot, your scalp, a temple, or the back of the neck, the top of a shoulder, etc. (Avoid massaging the front of the neck. Also avoid massaging injured or numb body parts, or bruised, inflamed, or recently surgically operated on areas, or varicose veins. Also stop if the massage makes the anxiety symptoms worse, or makes you feel bad in any way, such as painful, dizzy, tingly, etc.) Some massage therapies are super aggressive, like Rolfing, some are fairly aggressive still like Deep Tissue, some are medium-aggressive, like Thai massage, and some, like Swedish Massage, are quite gentle. Choose the level that feels right for you. You’ve got lots of other options for the body too, like heat, pressure, a weighted blanket, darkness, your favorite calming music, or a massage gun if you’re careful with it, etc. Use whatever actually helps you, and don’t go surrounding the anxiety with a heap of wellness stuff.
why: A reader who books a massage to calm down knows the styles run from forceful to gentle, and picks the level.
doubt: I put it after the bracketed cautions and before 'You’ve got lots of other options', so the cautions stay next to the body parts they are about; straight after 'Maybe get a massage' is the other place it could go. The paragraph was already long and this adds two sentences. The source doesn't say to pick a gentle style for anxiety, only to choose the level that feels right, so this doesn't either.
